# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
The comment does useful forensic work on the Halden pilot. The microdata findings in sections 1–4 are valuable, and two of them (that most withdrawals came after the schedule began, and the manager-versus-records gap) are things nobody could see from the working paper alone. The trouble is that the conclusion goes well past the evidence. The headline claim, that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact," is contradicted by the randomised trial the comment itself cites.

## 1. Arithmetic: mostly right, a few errors

**Correct:**

| Figure | Check |
|---|---|
| Table 2, as reported | 98.7 / 0.8 = +23.4% |
| Table 2, records + scheduled hours | 95.1 / 0.8 = +18.9% |
| Table 2, manager index + actual hours | 98.4 / 0.859 = +14.6% |
| Table 2, records + actual hours | 95.4 / 0.861 = +10.8% |
| Actual hours, 27 organisations | 34.6 / 40.3 = −14.1% |
| Actual hours, 17 organisations | 34.8 / 40.4 = −13.9% |
| Real revenue | 1.014 / 1.041 = −2.6% |

**Errors:**
- **The hours breakdown doesn't add up.** Section 3 says actual hours exceeded the 32 scheduled because of +0.7 hours per day on four days (2.8 h) plus 1.6 h on the day off. That gives about 36.4 h, not the reported 34.6 h. The reported total implies only about 2.6 extra hours a week, so either the daily figure or the weekly total is wrong.
- **The energy extrapolation is off.** A straight line from 0.61 SD at month 3 to 0.29 SD at month 6 reaches zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten." Extrapolating from two points is weak in any case (see §4).
- **The Abstract mis-states what was corrected.**
  - It says "correcting the first three" problems. The first three are attrition, output measure and hours. Table 2 corrects only output and hours, so **attrition is never corrected or bounded**.
  - It says four problems "account for most of the reported gain," but the revenue problem doesn't enter the per-hour calculation at all. Only two of the four problems are actually measured against the gain.

## 2. Problems with the corrections themselves

- **Each row of Table 2 uses a different sample (61, 23, 27, 17 organisations).** The fall from 23.4% to 10.8% therefore mixes the effect of the correction with the effect of changing samples. The clean comparison is to compute all four specifications within the same 17 organisations. The baseline row (manager index ÷ 0.8) is the most important one to add.
- **Records are treated as the truth, but some aren't output measures.** "Billable hours delivered" measures input. It will fall roughly in line with hours cut, whatever happens to productivity. Organisations that used it will show a lower record-based index almost automatically. Other record types (tickets closed, units) ignore complexity and quality, which managers may legitimately have taken into account. The fact that the manager figure was higher in 19 of 23 organisations does suggest optimism, but the 3.8-point gap partly reflects which measure was used.
- **Weighting isn't stated.** The original paper used employee-weighted means. The comment doesn't say whether Table 1 and Table 2 match that.
- **No uncertainty is reported.** The comment rightly faults the pilot for its weaknesses, yet gives no confidence intervals itself. A gain of 10.8% based on 17 organisations needs one.
- **Attrition could be partly quantified.** Seven of the nine withdrawers left after the schedule began. If the microdata include their monthly output indices, an intention-to-treat estimate or a bounding exercise is possible.
  - Example: if the nine averaged 85, the overall mean would fall by roughly 1.8 points.
  - Without some such calculation, attrition contributes rhetorically but not numerically.
- **An implication worth adding.** Counting the post-start withdrawals, about 56 of the 68 organisations that actually started continued, or 82%, not the 92% the pilot reported.

## 3. The central overreach: Varden contradicts "entirely an artifact"

The comment names three sources of artifact: selection, measurement and novelty.

**The Varden case-processing stratum largely rules out the first two:**
- offices were randomly assigned, so there was no self-selection;
- output came from administrative records;
- hours came from timesheets;
- there was a control group.

It still found output per actual hour up **12.5% (CI 6.9 to 18.4)** at nine months.

The comment calls Varden's counter-office result "the most reliable finding in the literature." It does not mention the case-processing result from the same trial, which runs against its conclusion. Citing only one half of the trial is the most serious problem in the piece.

**Novelty is not well supported either:**
- Varden ran for nine months, which is past the comment's own projected fade point.
- Varden staff didn't choose the change, so the "change that staff chose, welcomed" setting doesn't apply.
- Varden's control offices also knew they were being evaluated, which partly offsets an observation effect.

## 4. The novelty argument skips the obvious test

The argument rests on a self-reported energy score, but the claim is about **output**. The pilot collected a monthly output index, so the microdata should show directly whether output per hour fell over the six months. That is the natural test of novelty, and the comment doesn't run it. Fading energy does not show that productivity faded.

"The burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter" is fair. But "entirely an artifact" is itself a positive claim and carries the same burden.

## 5. Section 7 misrepresents the Varden meetings analysis

- **Timing is wrong.** The comment says the meetings data were "selected for analysis after the results were known." Varden collected them in month six, during the trial, at managers' request.
- **The authors' claim is overstated.** Varden's authors said the analysis was unregistered, that seven offices "cannot establish a mechanism," and that they had registered a confirmatory test. The comment argues against a stronger claim than they made.
- **Inconsistent standards.** The comment dismisses an exploratory correlation as post hoc, then offers its own post hoc novelty explanation built on two survey data points.
- **Corroborating evidence is ignored.** In the Halden pilot, 47 of 58 managers independently mentioned meeting cuts.
- **Meeting cuts would be a real gain, not an artifact.** Removing low-value time is a real productivity gain, though perhaps one that could be had without cutting hours. That is a substantive point about mechanism, not a measurement error. Varden's own figures suggest it could explain much of the case-processing gain.

## 6. The conclusion contradicts the Data note

The Data note says the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole." The Conclusion then generalises to "reduced-hours schemes" in general. Both cannot stand.

The retail comparison is also thin. It sets an 11.2% fall across three Halden organisations against Varden's 11.4%, but these are different measures in different settings. The near-identical numbers are a coincidence, not corroboration.

## 7. What holds up

- **Attrition.** The pilot described the withdrawals as happening during preparation, but seven of the nine came after the schedule began, and most cited workload. That is a significant misreport, and the comment is right to raise it.
- **Manager-reported output.** The tendency to overstate output relative to records is well documented, with the caveat about input-type records in §2.
- **Hours.** Scheduled hours overstate the reduction by about six percentage points in the organisations that tracked time.
- **Revenue.** Adjusting for inflation turns the reported growth into a fall of about 2.6%.
- **The sector claim.** Saying the model is sector-general is an artifact of the per-hour metric.
- **Recommendations.** These are sensible.

## A defensible conclusion

> Correcting for output measurement and actual hours reduces the Halden per-hour gain from 23.4% to about 11% in the 17 organisations where both corrections are possible, before any adjustment for attrition, which likely reduces it further. Whether the residual persists is unknown. The only randomised evidence finds a gain of similar size (12.5%) in backlog-type work at nine months, and a clear loss of output per employee in coverage-bound work.

That version is still a strong critique of the pilot, and a referee could not easily dismiss it.

I can draft a referee report or a reply from the Halden authors' side if that would help.
